```{python}
#| eval: false
import pandas as pd

# Import Stata dataset
hrs = pd.read_stata(
    "randhrs1992_2022v2.dta",
    convert_categoricals=False
)

# Standardize column names to lowercase
hrs.columns = hrs.columns.str.lower()

# Keep identifiers
id_cols = ["hhidpn", "rahhidpn", "hhid", "pn"]

# Survey weight and design variables
survey_cols = [
    "r16wtresp",
    "r16wtcrnh",
    "raestrat",
    "raehsamp",
    "stratum",
    "secu"
]

# Keep identifiers, survey design, all-wave, and Wave 16 variables
selected_cols = [
    col for col in hrs.columns
    if col in id_cols
    or col in survey_cols
    or col.startswith(("ra", "sa", "ha", "r16", "s16", "h16"))
]

randhrs2022 = hrs[selected_cols].copy()

# Drop rows where all R16 and S16 values are NaN
rs16_cols = [
    col for col in randhrs2022.columns
    if col.startswith(("r16", "s16"))
]

randhrs2022 = randhrs2022.dropna(subset=rs16_cols, how="all")

# Export updated dataset
randhrs2022.to_csv("randhrs2022_v1.csv", index=False)

# Check results
print("Dataset shape:", randhrs2022.shape)

randhrs2022.head()
```

### 1.2 Import required library and dataset

```{r}
# Import required library
library(tidyverse)
library(survey)
library(srvyr)

# Import raw dataset
hrs <- read_csv("randhrs2022_v1.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

### 1.3 Set up survey weight design

```{r}
# Filter valid survey weights and create survey design
hrs_weight <- hrs %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(r16wtcrnh),
    r16wtcrnh > 0,
    !is.na(rastratum),
    !is.na(rasecu)
  ) %>%
  as_survey_design(
    ids = rasecu,
    strata = rastratum,
    weights = r16wtcrnh,
    nest = TRUE
  )

# Check sample size before and after filtering
nrow(hrs)
nrow(hrs_weight$variables)
```

### 1.3 Adjust relevant categorical levels

```{r}
# Recode relevant categorical variables
hrs_weight <- hrs_weight %>%
  mutate(
    r16sleeprt = factor(
      r16sleeprt,
      levels = c(3, 2, 1),
      labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")
    ),
    raeduc = factor(
      raeduc,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "GED",
        "High school graduate",
        "Some college",
        "College and above"
      )
    )
  )

# Inspect relevant variables
hrs_weight$variables %>%
  select(r16cog27, r16sleeprt, r16agey_e, raeduc) %>%
  glimpse()

# Check missing values (unweighted counts)
hrs_weight$variables %>%
  summarise(across(
    c(r16cog27, r16sleeprt, r16agey_e, raeduc),
    ~ sum(is.na(.x))
  ))
```

## 3. **Ordinal Regression and Diagnostics**

### 3.1 Model specification

As a complement to the linear model, we classify each respondent's 27-point cognitive score into the three Langa–Weir cognitive status categories commonly used with HRS data: dementia (0–6), cognitive impairment without dementia (CIND, 7–11), and normal cognition (12–27). These categories have a natural order, but the distances between them are not equal, so we fit a survey-weighted proportional odds (ordinal logistic) model:

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{logit}\, P(\text{Status}_i \le k)
= \theta_k - \big[\,& \beta_1 \text{Sleep\_M}_i + \beta_2 \text{Sleep\_H}_i + \beta_3 \text{Age10}_i \\
&+ \beta_4 \text{GED}_i + \beta_5 \text{HighSchool}_i + \beta_6 \text{SomeCollege}_i + \beta_7 \text{CollegeAbove}_i \\
&+ \beta_8 (\text{Sleep\_M}_i \times \text{Age10}_i) + \beta_9 (\text{Sleep\_H}_i \times \text{Age10}_i) \big]
\end{aligned}$$

where:

- $k \in \{\text{Dementia}, \text{CIND}\}$ indexes the two cut points, and $\theta_k$ are the cut-point intercepts.
- $\text{Age10}_i = (\text{Age}_i - 65)/10$, so the sleep coefficients describe a 65-year-old and the age coefficient describes a 10-year difference in age.
- Sleep quality (reference: low) and education (reference: less than high school) are coded as in the linear model.
- $e^{\beta}$ is an odds ratio: values above 1 mean higher odds of being in a **better** cognitive category.
- $e^{\beta_2}$ is the odds ratio for high vs. low sleep quality at age 65; the odds ratio at other ages is $e^{\beta_2 + \beta_9 \times \text{Age10}}$.

The model uses the combined community and nursing-home weight (`r16wtcrnh`) with HRS strata and sampling error computation units, so estimates represent the U.S. population covered by HRS Wave 16 and standard errors account for the complex survey design.

```{r}
#| include: false
# ============================================================
# 3. Ordinal regression (Chen)
# Requires: hrs_weight (survey design built in Section 1.3),
#           with r16sleeprt and raeduc already recoded as factors
# ============================================================
library(MASS)   # polr(): unweighted ordinal model for comparison
library(car)    # vif(): multicollinearity check
# NOTE: MASS masks dplyr::select(); always write dplyr::select() below

# Add the ordinal outcome and centered age to the design
hrs_ord <- update(
  hrs_weight,
  cog_status = factor(
    case_when(
      r16cog27 <= 6  ~ "Dementia",   # Langa-Weir cutoffs
      r16cog27 <= 11 ~ "CIND",
      TRUE           ~ "Normal"
    ),
    levels  = c("Dementia", "CIND", "Normal"),
    ordered = TRUE                    # worst -> best
  ),
  age10 = (r16agey_e - 65) / 10       # 0 = age 65, 1 unit = 10 years
)

# Complete cases on model variables (subset() keeps the design correct)
hrs_ord <- subset(
  hrs_ord,
  !is.na(r16cog27) & !is.na(r16sleeprt) & !is.na(r16agey_e) & !is.na(raeduc)
)

n_ord <- nrow(hrs_ord$variables)

# Weighted distribution of cognitive status
status_pct <- prop.table(svytable(~ cog_status, hrs_ord)) * 100
```

```{r}
#| include: false
# Weighted proportional odds model with the sleep x age interaction
fit_ord <- svyolr(cog_status ~ r16sleeprt * age10 + raeduc, design = hrs_ord)

est  <- coef(fit_ord)
se   <- sqrt(diag(vcov(fit_ord)))
keep <- !grepl("\\|", names(est))      # drop cut points such as "Dementia|CIND"

# Readable labels for the report (no raw variable names)
term_labels <- c(
  "r16sleeprtMedium"           = "Medium sleep quality (vs. low)",
  "r16sleeprtHigh"             = "High sleep quality (vs. low)",
  "age10"                      = "Age (per 10 years)",
  "raeducGED"                  = "GED (vs. less than high school)",
  "raeducHigh school graduate" = "High school graduate",
  "raeducSome college"         = "Some college",
  "raeducCollege and above"    = "College and above",
  "r16sleeprtMedium:age10"     = "Medium sleep x Age (per 10 years)",
  "r16sleeprtHigh:age10"       = "High sleep x Age (per 10 years)"
)

or_table <- tibble(
  Term       = term_labels[names(est)[keep]],
  `Odds ratio` = exp(est[keep]),
  `95% CI`   = sprintf("%.2f, %.2f",
                       exp(est[keep] - 1.96 * se[keep]),
                       exp(est[keep] + 1.96 * se[keep])),
  `p-value`  = 2 * pnorm(-abs(est[keep] / se[keep]))
)

# Wald test for the sleep x age interaction as a whole
int_test <- regTermTest(fit_ord, ~ r16sleeprt:age10)
```

```{r}
# Table: odds ratios from the weighted ordinal model
or_table %>%
  mutate(
    `Odds ratio` = sprintf("%.2f", `Odds ratio`),
    `p-value`    = format.pval(`p-value`, digits = 2, eps = 0.001)
  ) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Survey-weighted proportional odds model: odds of being in a better cognitive status category"
  )
```

### 3.2 Predicted probabilities

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 6
# Predicted probability of normal cognition by age and sleep quality
# (education fixed at high school graduate), computed from the weighted model
beta <- est[keep]
zeta <- est[!keep]

pred_grid <- expand_grid(
  r16sleeprt = factor(c("Low", "Medium", "High"), levels = c("Low", "Medium", "High")),
  r16agey_e  = 55:90,
  raeduc     = factor("High school graduate", levels = levels(hrs_ord$variables$raeduc))
) %>%
  mutate(age10 = (r16agey_e - 65) / 10)

X <- model.matrix(~ r16sleeprt * age10 + raeduc, data = pred_grid)[, names(beta)]
pred_grid$p_normal <- 1 - plogis(zeta["CIND|Normal"] - drop(X %*% beta))

ggplot(pred_grid, aes(x = r16agey_e, y = p_normal, color = r16sleeprt)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent) +
  labs(
    title = "Predicted Probability of Normal Cognition",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Probability of normal cognition",
    color = "Sleep quality"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

### 3.3 Model assessment

```{r}
#| include: false
# (1) Proportional odds check: fit the two cumulative splits as separate
#     weighted binary logistic models and compare their odds ratios
hrs_ord <- update(
  hrs_ord,
  above_dementia = as.numeric(cog_status >= "CIND"),    # split 1: CIND or Normal vs. Dementia
  normal         = as.numeric(cog_status == "Normal")   # split 2: Normal vs. Dementia or CIND
)

fit_split1 <- svyglm(above_dementia ~ r16sleeprt * age10 + raeduc,
                     design = hrs_ord, family = quasibinomial())
fit_split2 <- svyglm(normal ~ r16sleeprt * age10 + raeduc,
                     design = hrs_ord, family = quasibinomial())

# (2) Unweighted ordinal model, to see how much the survey weights matter
fit_unw <- polr(cog_status ~ r16sleeprt * age10 + raeduc,
                data = hrs_ord$variables, Hess = TRUE)

# (3) Multicollinearity among main-effect predictors
vif_tab <- vif(lm(r16cog27 ~ r16sleeprt + age10 + raeduc, data = hrs_ord$variables))
```

```{r}
# Table: odds ratios across the ordinal model, the two binary splits,
# and the unweighted ordinal model
tibble(
  Term                    = term_labels[names(beta)],
  `Ordinal (weighted)`    = exp(beta),
  `CIND+ vs. Dementia`    = exp(coef(fit_split1))[names(beta)],
  `Normal vs. CIND/Dem.`  = exp(coef(fit_split2))[names(beta)],
  `Ordinal (unweighted)`  = exp(coef(fit_unw))[names(beta)]
) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    digits  = 2,
    caption = "Proportional odds check and weighted vs. unweighted comparison (odds ratios)"
  )
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-width: 7
# Survey-weighted binned residual plots for the two cumulative splits
# (each split of the ordinal outcome is a binary logistic model)
binned_resid <- function(fit, label, n_bins = 40) {
  tibble(
    fitted = fitted(fit),                               # predicted probability
    resid  = fit$y - fitted(fit),                       # observed minus predicted
    w      = weights(fit$survey.design, "sampling")     # survey weights
  ) %>%
    mutate(bin = ntile(fitted, n_bins)) %>%             # group by predicted probability
    group_by(bin) %>%
    summarise(
      mean_fitted = weighted.mean(fitted, w),
      mean_resid  = weighted.mean(resid, w),
      se          = 2 * sqrt(mean_fitted * (1 - mean_fitted) / n()),  # +/- 2 SE bounds
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    mutate(split = label)
}

binned_df <- bind_rows(
  binned_resid(fit_split1, "CIND or normal vs. dementia"),
  binned_resid(fit_split2, "Normal vs. CIND or dementia")
)

# Share of bins inside the +/- 2 SE bounds, used in the text below
pct_inside <- binned_df %>%
  group_by(split) %>%
  summarise(inside = 100 * mean(abs(mean_resid) <= se), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(binned_df, aes(x = mean_fitted, y = mean_resid)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line(aes(y = se),  linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_line(aes(y = -se), linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~ split, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Binned Residual Plots",
    x = "Average predicted probability",
    y = "Average residual"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Assumptions.** The proportional odds model assumes (1) an ordered outcome, (2) that each predictor has the same odds ratio at every cut point (proportional odds), (3) independent observations after accounting for the survey design, and (4) no severe multicollinearity. Independence is addressed by the design-based standard errors (strata and clusters), rather than by assuming a simple random sample.

**Assessment.**

- *Proportional odds:* We compared each predictor's odds ratio from the ordinal model with the odds ratios from two separate weighted logistic regressions, one for each cut point. For the main sleep and age effects, the second split (normal vs. CIND or dementia) closely matches the ordinal model, while the first split (any cognition above dementia vs. dementia) gives somewhat smaller sleep effects. Because only about 3% of the weighted population is classified as dementia, this split is estimated with much less precision, so we treat the proportional odds assumption as approximately reasonable for our main conclusions, but note it as a limitation.
- *Interaction:* A design-based Wald test indicates that the sleep × age interaction improves the model (F = `r sprintf("%.2f", int_test$Ftest)`, p = `r format.pval(int_test$p, digits = 2)`).
- *Model fit (binned residuals):* For each cumulative split, we grouped respondents into 40 bins by predicted probability and plotted the survey-weighted average residuals. About `r sprintf("%.0f", pct_inside$inside[1])`% of bins for the first split and `r sprintf("%.0f", pct_inside$inside[2])`% for the second split fall within the ±2 standard error bounds, and the residuals are scattered around zero without a systematic pattern, suggesting no major lack of fit.
- *Multicollinearity:* Generalized VIFs for sleep quality, age, and education are all close to 1 (maximum `r sprintf("%.2f", max(vif_tab[, 1]))`), so collinearity is not a concern.
- *Survey weights:* Unweighted estimates point in the same direction but are somewhat smaller for high sleep quality, which supports using the weighted model for population-level inference.

### 3.4 Interpretation

The analytic sample includes `r format(n_ord, big.mark = ",")` respondents with complete data. After weighting, about `r sprintf("%.1f", status_pct["Normal"])`% of the population has normal cognition, `r sprintf("%.1f", status_pct["CIND"])`% has CIND, and `r sprintf("%.1f", status_pct["Dementia"])`% falls in the dementia range.

Holding education constant, at age 65 respondents who report high sleep quality have about `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(beta["r16sleeprtHigh"]))` times the odds of being in a better cognitive category than respondents with low sleep quality. The difference between medium and low sleep quality is smaller and not statistically significant. The significant high sleep × age interaction (OR = `r sprintf("%.2f", exp(beta["r16sleeprtHigh:age10"]))` per 10 years) indicates that the advantage associated with high sleep quality becomes smaller at older ages, which is also visible in the predicted probability plot, where the sleep-quality lines converge after about age 80. Education shows the strongest association with cognitive status, with college graduates having much higher odds of a better cognitive category than respondents without a high school diploma. These are cross-sectional associations and should not be interpreted as causal effects of sleep on cognition.

### Dataset Option 2 (For Reference to be deleted later)

------------------------------------------------------------------------

**Project Title:** Remember Me: Is Better Sleep Associated with Better Cognition?

**Data citation (use APA formatting or something similar):** Health and Retirement Study. (2026). *RAND HRS longitudinal file 2022 (Version 2).* University of Michigan. <https://hrsdata.isr.umich.edu/data-products/rand-hrs-longitudinal-file-2022>

**Original data collection date (when was the dataset published?):** Oct 2026

**Data pull date (when did you download the data you will use?):** 4 Nov 2026

------------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 1 Research Question

How do cognitive scores differ across high, medium, and low sleep quality, after accounting for age and education, and does the association between sleep quality and cognitive performance vary by age?

#### 2 Study Population

The observation unit is an individual respondent in the Health and Retirement Study (HRS) across 16 waves. The study is a longitudinal household survey conducted by the University of Michigan's Institute for Social Research and collects repeated survey information on health, cognition, employment, finances, and other aspects of aging in the United States.

For this analysis, we will focus on the data in the latest wave 16 in 2022.

#### 4 Statistical Analysis Plan

**4.1 Exploratory Data Analysis**

Cognitive score is a continuous variable ranging from 0–27, so we will use a histogram to examine its distribution. Sleep quality is a categorical factor with three levels, so we will compare cognitive score distributions across sleep-quality groups using boxplots.

We will also examine the distributions of age and education and use summary statistics to describe the sample. For our hypothesis, we assume that respondents who report better sleep quality will have higher cognitive scores. It is also expected that this relationship may differ by age, while accounting for education, since cognitive performance generally varies across age and educational background.

**4.2 Statistical Model (write in mathematical notation and define each term)**

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{CognitiveScore}_i
=&\ \beta_0
+ \beta_1 \text{Sleep\_M}_i
+ \beta_2 \text{Sleep\_H}_i
+ \beta_3 \text{Age}_i \\
&+ \beta_4 \text{GED}_i
+ \beta_5 \text{HighSchool}_i
+ \beta_6 \text{SomeCollege}_i
+ \beta_7 \text{CollegeAbove}_i \\
&+ \beta_8(\text{Sleep\_M}_i \times \text{Age}_i)
+ \beta_9(\text{Sleep\_H}_i \times \text{Age}_i)
+ \epsilon_i
\end{aligned}$$

Where:

- $\text{CognitiveScore}_i$ = Cognitive score for respondent $i$, ranging from 0 to 27.
- $\text{Sleep\_M}_i$ = 1 if respondent $i$ has **medium sleep quality**, 0 otherwise.
- $\text{Sleep\_H}_i$ = 1 if respondent $i$ has **high sleep quality**, 0 otherwise.
- $\text{Age}_i$ = Respondent's age in years.
- $\text{GED}_i$ = 1 if respondent $i$ has a GED, 0 otherwise.
- $\text{HighSchool}_i$ = 1 if respondent $i$ is a high school graduate, 0 otherwise.
- $\text{SomeCollege}_i$ = 1 if respondent $i$ has some college education, 0 otherwise.
- $\text{CollegeAbove}_i$ = 1 if respondent $i$ has college education or above, 0 otherwise.
- $\text{Sleep\_M}_i \times \text{Age}_i$ = Interaction between medium sleep quality and age.
- $\text{Sleep\_H}_i \times \text{Age}_i$ = Interaction between high sleep quality and age.
- $\epsilon_i$ = Error term for respondent $i$.

**4.2 Rationale for the statistical model**

We will use multiple linear regression because the outcome, cognitive score, is a numeric variable ranging from 0 to 27. This approach allows us to estimate differences in cognitive score across sleep-quality groups while also accounting for age and education. However, because the cognitive score is bounded between 0 and 27, we will assess whether the assumptions of linear regression are appropriate, particularly the normality and equal variance of the residuals. If these assumptions are substantially violated, we will consider an alternative generalized linear modeling approach that better accommodates the distribution of the cognitive score.

**4.3 Model Assumptions**

- Linearity - The relationship between predicted value and the predictors is linear

- Independence - The observations are independent of one another.

- Normality - The residuals are approximately normally distributed.

- Equal variance - The residuals have approximately constant variance across predicted values.

**4.4 Model Assessment (how will you assess the assumptions and model performance?)**

- Linearity - Assess the residuals vs. fitted plot for a random cloud with no clear pattern.

- Equal variance - Assess the residuals vs. fitted plot for a constant spread across the red line with no fanning behavior.

- Independence - Check that the residuals do not show obvious clustering or systematic patterns.

- Normality - Assess the Q-Q plot to see whether the residuals approximately follow a 45-degree diagonal line.

**Outcome:** Cognitive scores range from 0 to 27, with a mean of 15.05 (SD = 4.63). The distribution is roughly centered around a score of about 15, with relatively few observations at the lowest and highest values.

**Key predictor:** Among respondents with available sleep-quality information, 49.1% reported high sleep quality, 33.7% reported medium sleep quality, and 17.1% reported low sleep quality.

**Key relationship**

- Based on the box plot, cognitive scores appear to be slightly higher among respondents who report better sleep quality. Respondents with high sleep quality have a slightly higher median cognitive score than those with medium or low sleep quality.

- Scatter plot also demonstrates a clearer negative relationship with age. Overall, older respondents tend to have lower cognitive scores on average.

**Missing Variables:** Many observations are missing for Wave 16 variables because not all respondents participated in the latest wave. We will account for this when defining the analytic sample and report how many observations remain after restricting the analysis to respondents with complete data for the variables included in the model.
